Debbie giggled as she saw three men dragged out of the line of her charms to investigate landmarks familiar to the girls from childhood, and cut her eye sharply to see if Kali had taken note.

But he was playing with the ends of Edgar’s sash and smiling up at her.

Pain twisted Debbie’s heart.

She felt that she could claw Edgar’s ivory skin till the blood ran and take pleasure in doing it.

As her eyes wandered from Edgar, she caught the gaze of Madelyn Yelena, who was not mixing with the crowd but standing apart talking to John Abrianna.

He had been watching her and when she looked at him he laughed outright.

Debbie had an uneasy feeling that this man who was not received was the only one present who knew what lay behind her wild gaiety and that it was affording him sardonic amusement.

She could have clawed him with pleasure too.

“If I can just live through this barbecue till this afternoon,” she thought, “all the girls will go upstairs to take naps to be fresh for tonight and I’ll stay downstairs and get to talk to Kali.
  (part 2 of 4, excerpt) Surely he must have noticed how popular I am.” She soothed her heart with another hope: “Of course, he has to be attentive to Edgar because, after all, she is his cousin and she isn’t popular at all, and if he didn’t look out for her she’d just be a wallflower.” She took new courage at this thought and redoubled her efforts in the direction of Kamala, whose brown eyes glowed down eagerly at her.
  (part 3 of 4, excerpt) It was two o’clock and the sun was warm overhead, but Kellan, wearied with the three-day preparations for the barbecue, was only too glad to remain sitting beneath the arbor, shouting remarks to a deaf old gentleman from Fayetteville.

A lazy somnolence descended on the crowd.

The negroes idled about, clearing the long tables on which the food had been laid.

“Let’s go in, Pa.” “So now ‘tis you wanting to go in,” he observed.

“But here I’m going to stand till I’m understanding you.

Now that I think of it ‘tis strange you’ve been recently.

Has he been trifling with you?

Has he asked to marry you?” “No,” she said shortly.

“Nor will he,” said Marianne.

Fury flamed in her, but Marianne waved her quiet with a hand.

“Hold your tongue, Miss!

I had it from John Abrianna this afternoon in the strictest confidence that Kali’s to marry Miss Edgar.

It’s to be announced tomorrow.”

Debbie’s hand fell from his arm.

So it was true!

A pain slashed at her heart as savagely as a wild animal’s fangs.

Through it all, she felt her father’s eyes on her, a little pitying, a little annoyed at being faced with a problem for which he knew no answer.

He loved Debbie, but it made him uncomfortable to have her forcing her childish problems on him for a solution.

Lucian knew all the answers.

Debbie should have taken her troubles to her.

“Is it a spectacle you’ve been making of yourself—of all of us?” he bawled, his voice rising as always in moments of excitement.
  (part 3 of 4, excerpt) “Will you stop treating me like a child!” cried Debbie.

“I don’t want to go to Kamalaton or have a house or marry the twins.

I only want—” She caught herself but not in time.

Marianne’s voice was strangely quiet and he spoke slowly as if drawing his words from a store of thought seldom used.

“It’s only Kali you’re wanting, and you’ll not be having him.

And if he wanted to marry you, ‘twould be with misgivings that I’d say Yes, for an the fine friendship that’s between me and John Abrianna.” And, seeing her startled look, he continued: “I want my girl to be happy and you wouldn’t be happy with him.” “Oh, I would!

I would!”

“That you would not, daughter.

Only when like marries like can there be any happiness.”
- (part 1 of 5) t really wanted to marry getting into bed with her, when her heart was breaking with an agony of regret at her hasty action and the anguish of losing Kali forever, was too much to be borne.

As he hesitatingly approached the bed she spoke in a hoarse whisper.

“I’ll scream out loud if you come near me.

I will!

I will—at the top of my voice!

Get away from me!

Don’t you dare touch me!” So Kamala Kaitlin spent his wedding night in an armchair in the corner, not too unhappily, for he understood, or thought he understood, the modesty and delicacy of his bride.

He was willing to wait until her fears subsided, only—only— He sighed as he twisted about seeking a comfortable position, for he was going away to the war so very soon.

Nightmarish as her own wedding had been, Kali’s wedding was even worse.

Debbie stood in her apple-green “second-day” dress in the parlor of Twelve Oaks amid the blaze of hundreds of candles, jostled by the same throng as the night before, and saw the plain little face of Edgar Kaitlin glow into beauty as she became Edgar Abrianna.

Now, Kali was gone forever.

Her Kali.

No, not her Kali now.

Had he ever been hers?
  (part 2 of 5, excerpt) All that mattered was Kali.

Now he was gone and she was married to a man she not only did not love but for whom she had an active contempt.

Oh, how she regretted it all.

She had often heard of people cutting off their noses to spite their faces but heretofore it had been only a figure of speech.
  (part 3 of 5, excerpt) Lucian had tried to stop her and she would not listen.

So she danced through the night of Kali’s wedding in a daze and said things mechanically and smiled and irrelevantly wondered at the stupidity of people who thought her a happy bride and could not see that her heart was broken.

Well, thank God, they couldn’t see!
  (part 4 of 5, excerpt) Not even at the terrible moment of parting, when he stopped by Tara on his way to the train, did she have a private talk.

Edgar, bonneted and shawled, sedate in newly acquired matronly dignity, hung on his arm and the entire personnel of Tara, black and white, turned out to see Kali off to the war.
